name: Lena Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a researcher from the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI companies, unions and government. Your answers are confidential. What is a usual workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, with a bachelor’s degree and a professional accountancy qualification, and I prepare accounts and tax returns for small firms, including cafés. I have done this for years and can handle ordinary files, though a senior checks hard cases. I use the firm’s approved AI sorter every day and still match the results to receipts and bank statements. I enjoy untangling a café’s missing card receipts, but chasing a last invoice after school pickup wears me down.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Pavel, my partner, drives a school bus, and our two school-age children bring home a steady flow of costs. We have a mortgage, my pay is low for an experienced accountant, and savings cover less than a month of expenses. There are few similar jobs nearby, so I like learning early but need the wage we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a little software help is useful when the client still gets a checked tax return. The café owners I work with often send the last invoice after we think the file is finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage is low for an experienced accountant, and we have less than a month of expenses saved against the mortgage. I like the tools, but small time savings do not make a school bill disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep using the approved AI sorter I use every day to group café receipts, checking each total against the bank statement. In the first year I would transfer 25 from my pay into a school-expense account each month while my hours hold, and keep the same client files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the household cushion, although the work itself stays steady. The bank balance is a bigger worry than the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a late invoice do to your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I reopen the return, check whether the invoice belongs in that tax period, and ask the owner where it was paid. My senior reviews the final change because a hurried fix can cause another mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the 25 come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring coffee from home and move the amount after payday, not just promise to spend less. My partner Pavel drives a school bus, and we count only his scheduled hours in the budget.

say: I would welcome **small software help** if the final return stays checked.
I would tell café clients **late invoices** still need a person to question them.
think: My **low pay** and sub-month reserve already strain the mortgage.
Small time savings do not cover **school bills**.
do: Keep using the **daily approved sorter** and compare café totals with bank statements.
Deposit **25 monthly** into school-expense savings while my hours hold.
feel: I feel **anxious** about our cushion despite stable account work.
S0.quote: The bank balance is a bigger worry than the software.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** is checked against bank records and senior review, not a claim that the tool is always right.
The **25 monthly deposit** comes from coffee she will stop buying and depends on full hours.

steps.text: Keep sorting café receipts with approved AI and checking bank totals
Deposit 25 from pay into school-expense account monthly while hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues the firm should show us which returns the new tool drafts and where it still needs a checker. A faster file is not an excuse to hide a wrong number from a café owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing tax notes and checking invoices are much of my day, so I could lose paid hours even though I use AI daily. With less than a month saved and few nearby firms, that is a real risk, but I can learn the new process quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask to test the approved tax-drafting tool on five closed café returns during paid hours and share the correction list with my senior. I would move the planned family weekend trip money into the bill account instead of paying the deposit; if my hours are cut in the first year, I would apply to an advertised local accounts post only with written salary and hours at least equal to now, keeping paid shifts until an offer and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible cut, not sure that it will happen. I know the tools, but that does not mean the firm will keep all my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What error would you look for first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for food bought for a family meal that the tool treated as a café supply. I would show the original receipt to my senior before correcting the draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the trip money as cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have a mortgage and two children in school, so I want that unspent money available for bills. I am not calling it new savings; it is money we had planned to spend.

say: I would ask the firm to show **software-drafted returns** and named checks.
I would tell clients a **fast file** still needs correct figures.
think: My **tax-note hours** could shrink despite daily AI use.
Our **thin reserve** and few local firms make a cut serious.
do: Test **five closed café returns** in the approved drafting tool during paid hours with senior review.
Keep **unspent trip money** available for bills rather than paying the deposit.
After lost hours, apply for **advertised accounts work** with written equal pay and hours; retain shifts until start date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost hours while still able to learn.
S1.quote: I know the tools, but that does not mean the firm will keep all my hours.
fieldNote: Her **AI fluency** does not erase exposure to a paid-hour cut in desk-based tax work.
She describes **retained trip cash** as money not yet spent, and will search only after a cut while protecting current wages.

steps.text: Test approved tax drafting on five closed café returns during paid senior review
Keep unspent trip deposit money for bills instead of booking
Apply for advertised accounts post after cuts with written equal pay/hours; retain shifts until start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 reaches our tax and accounts desks in 2028, before capable robots arrive around 2031. The firm should tell staff the hours it expects to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my invoice checks and tax drafts to go when cheaper AGI can do the thinking. Daily AI use makes me faster now, but it cannot replace a wage when we have less than a month saved and few nearby jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for written hours notice and cancel the children’s paid after-school club from next term only after my sister confirms replacement pickups, keeping the fee for the mortgage. If my hours fall in the first year after 2028, I would apply to advertised local accounting posts with written pay and hours at least equal to mine; if none opens, I would ask Pavel whether confirmed extra school-bus runs can cover the next mortgage payment while I keep any paid tax work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the likely loss of our wage. The timetable is short and the mortgage is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can Pavel get extra runs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pavel sometimes covers another driver, but the school must confirm the route and paid hours. We would also need my sister to collect our children on those afternoons; I would ask before counting the bus pay. If nobody confirms replacement pickup, the after-school club stays in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a hands-on café job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have helped a client count stock once, but I am not a cook or a café manager. A physical stock count might buy time until capable robots around 2031, but I would need a paid opening and childcare before moving.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches tax desks before capable robots.
I would demand **written hours notice** from the firm.
think: I expect most **invoice checks and drafts** to disappear in 2028.
Daily AI skill cannot replace a **household wage** with no cushion.
do: Cancel **paid after-school club** next term only with confirmed replacement pickups, retaining the fee for the mortgage.
After lost hours, apply for **advertised accounting posts** with written equal pay and hours.
If none opens, ask **partner Pavel** about confirmed paid bus runs and childcare while retaining tax hours.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely wage loss and mortgage pressure.
S2.quote: Daily AI use makes me faster now, but it cannot replace a wage when we have less than a month saved and few nearby jobs.
fieldNote: Her **desk tasks** change with AGI in 2028; occasional physical stock counts are not a secure replacement once capable robots arrive later.
The **extra bus income** requires a confirmed paid route and her sister’s childcare; she retains paid tax hours during the search.

steps.text: Cancel after-school club next term only with confirmed replacement pickup; retain fee for mortgage
Apply to advertised accounting posts after cuts with written equal pay/hours while keeping paid tax work
Ask Pavel about confirmed paid bus runs and sister’s childcare if no vacancy opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2031 gives us time to build a paid client service before simple tax drafts change. Robots around 2034 are later than our desk deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let me learn how to reconcile café stock counts with accounts, though I expect routine invoice checking to shrink in 2031. I cannot spend our mortgage money on a private course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask my manager for one paid supervised café stock-count visit each month, with childcare arranged, to learn the link between goods and the accounts. I would save 55 monthly from my pay while both wages hold; in the first year after 2031, if my tax hours fall, I would take a vacant paid inventory-and-accounts role only with written salary and hours at least equal to now, or keep any paid returns while applying to advertised nearby firms. I would keep any current paid work until the replacement start date is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but the extra years make a supervised test possible. A role involving stock still needs a real wage and may face robots around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you count at a café?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check drinks and food stock against invoices while the café owner and senior reviewer watch, then correct the book entries. I would not claim I can run the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager declines the visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking tax returns and ask my senior to show me an old stock worksheet during paid office time. I would not do free weekend counts just to look keen.

say: I would propose **paid supervised stock visits** before 2031.
I would remind staff **2034 robots** may reach physical stock work later.
think: I need **paid learning**, not a course bought with mortgage cash.
do: Learn **monthly stock visits** with paid supervision, approval and childcare; if denied, keep returns and study old worksheets during paid hours.
Save **55 monthly** while both wages hold.
Take a **vacant paid inventory role** after cuts with written equal pay/hours and confirmed start; otherwise search while retaining paid returns.
feel: I feel **anxious** about income, with time to test a paid path.
S3.quote: A role involving stock still needs a real wage and may face robots around 2034.
fieldNote: Her **stock-count plan** learns a related hands-on task under café-owner and senior supervision, with childcare and paid time.
If visits are **denied**, she keeps paid returns and studies an old worksheet during office hours before seeking a vacancy.

steps.text: Learn on approved paid supervised monthly stock visits with childcare arranged
Save 55 monthly while both household wages hold
Take vacant paid inventory after cuts with written equal pay/hours, confirmed start; otherwise search while employed
Keep paid returns and study old stock worksheets during paid hours if visits denied

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives families a decade to build reserves and the firm time to pay for real training. The tax screens change in 2036, before capable robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years might let us reach four months of expenses in cash and get the children through school. I still expect the tax checking I do to shrink in 2036, and the stock work may not last once robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the café tax files and ask for a paid supervised stock visit each quarter if the manager and client agree and childcare is covered. I would build a four-month cash reserve with 75 monthly deposits while both wages hold; in the first year after 2036, if tax hours fall, I would take a vacant paid inventory role only with written equal salary and hours, or keep remaining account work while applying to advertised local firms. I would keep any current paid work until the replacement start date is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about our thin cash reserve now, even with a long runway. Building a four-month reserve needs our wages to stay intact long enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy stock-count equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the client has what we need for counting, and we have too little cash for a speculative kit. I would wait for paid demand before spending on anything beyond travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your children about the future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them to learn a useful task properly and keep a person who can check their work. A machine can make a quick draft, but someone still has to live with the bill.

say: I would use the **decade** to build savings and test paid stock work.
I would note **2039 robots** may reach the stock-count work later.
think: My **tax checks** may shrink after thinking AGI reaches desk work in 2036.
A **four-month reserve** needs both wages to hold.
do: Keep **café tax files** and learn on paid supervised stock visits only with manager, client and childcare approval.
Deposit **75 monthly** toward four months cash while both wages hold.
Take a **vacant paid inventory role** after cuts with written equal pay/hours and confirmed start; otherwise search while retaining paid returns.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current cash, despite a longer runway.
S4.quote: Building a four-month reserve needs our wages to stay intact long enough.
fieldNote: Her **ten-year plan** still begins with less than one month saved, so current mortgage risk shapes the mood.
She refuses **speculative equipment** spending and requires paid demand, supervision, client consent and childcare for stock visits.

steps.text: Learn on paid supervised stock visit only with manager, client and childcare approval
Deposit 75 monthly toward four months cash while both wages hold
Take vacant paid inventory after cuts with written equal pay/hours, confirmed start; otherwise search while employed
Keep paid café tax files if stock visits do not open

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my tax checks could disappear before we have even a mortgage payment saved. Written hours notice, paid supervised learning and an actual vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether using AI every day makes me less worried. A faster invoice draft does not pay for the children’s school bus or the mortgage.

headlineQuote: A faster invoice draft does not pay for the children’s school bus or the mortgage.
portrait: At **43**, Lena is an experienced accountant with a bachelor’s degree and professional qualification who handles café files.
She and **partner Pavel** have two school-age children, a mortgage, low pay and less than one month saved.
She uses **AI daily** but checks receipts, and few local accounting jobs are available.
The **2028 deadline** threatens tax checks; longer runways allow supervised stock work and conditional cash deposits.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her tax-checking hours before the household saves one mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written hours notice**, paid supervised learning and a real vacancy.
